text: Intimate partner violence (IPV) is a leading cause of homelessness and a serious threat to public health and well-being.
label: BACKGROUND

text: To determine whether the Domestic Violence Housing First (DVHF) model improves safety, housing stability, and mental health over 2 years.
label: CLAIM

text: This longitudinal comparative effectiveness study interviewed IPV survivors and reviewed their agency records.
label: BACKGROUND

text: All unstably housed or homeless IPV survivors entering domestic violence (DV) services were eligible to participate in the study, ensuring capture of typical variability in service delivery (eg, some survivors would enter services when agencies had the capacity to provide DVHF and others would receive services as usual [SAU]).
label: BACKGROUND

text: Clients from 5 DV agencies (3 rural and 2 urban) referred by agency staff in a Pacific Northwest state of the United States were assessed between July 17, 2017, and July 16, 2021.
label: BACKGROUND

text: Interviews were conducted in English or Spanish at entry into services (baseline) and at 6-, 12-, 18-, and 24-month follow-up visits.
label: BACKGROUND

text: The DVHF model was compared with SAU.
label: BACKGROUND

text: The baseline sample included 406 survivors (92.7% of 438 eligible).
label: BACKGROUND

text: Of the 375 participants retained at the 6-month follow-up (92.4% retention), 344 had received services and had complete data across all outcomes.
label: BACKGROUND

text: Three hundred sixty-three participants (89.4%) were retained at the 24-month follow-up.
label: BACKGROUND

text: The DVHF model has 2 components: housing-inclusive advocacy and flexible funding.
label: BACKGROUND

text: Main outcomes included housing stability, safety, and mental health, which were assessed using standardized measures.
label: BACKGROUND

text: Of the 344 participants (mean [SD] age, 34.6 [9.0] years) included in the analyses, 219 (63.7%) received DVHF and 125 (36.3%) received SAU.
label: BACKGROUND

text: Most participants identified as female (334 [97.1%]) and heterosexual (299 [86.9%]).
label: BACKGROUND

text: Two hundred twenty-one participants (64.2%) were from a racial and ethnic minority group.
label: BACKGROUND

text: Longitudinal linear mixed-effects models showed that receiving SAU was associated with greater housing instability (mean difference, 0.78 [95% CI, 0.42-1.14]), DV exposure (mean difference, 0.15 [95% CI, 0.05-0.26]), depression (mean difference, 1.35 [95% CI, 0.27-2.43]), anxiety (mean difference, 1.15 [95% CI, 0.11-2.19]), and posttraumatic stress disorder (mean difference, 0.54 [95% CI, 0.04-1.04]) compared with receiving the DVHF model.
label: CLAIM

text: Evidence in this comparative effectiveness study suggests that the DVHF model was more effective than SAU in improving the housing stability, safety, and mental health of survivors of IPV.
label: CLAIM

text: The DVHF’s amelioration of all of these interconnected public health issues—relatively quickly and with long-term continuance—will be of substantial interest to DV agencies and others working to support unstably housed IPV survivors.
label: BACKGROUND

text: Intimate partner violence (IPV) is a significant public health concern worldwide,[1] disproportionately affecting women.[2]
label: BACKGROUND

text: Intimate partner violence includes violence, abuse, and controlling behavior committed by a partner or former partner[3] and can result in long-lasting adverse mental health outcomes, including depression,[4] posttraumatic stress disorder (PTSD),[5] and anxiety.[6]
label: BACKGROUND

text: Intimate partner violence is also a leading cause of homelessness and housing instability.[7],[8],[9]
label: BACKGROUND

text: Given the link between IPV and housing instability, as well as the lack of affordable housing in the US,[10] domestic violence (DV) agencies are increasingly focusing on helping IPV survivors achieve stable housing along with long-term safety and well-being.[11],[12]
label: BACKGROUND

text: One intervention that is increasingly being implemented by DV agencies is the Domestic Violence Housing First (DVHF) model.
label: BACKGROUND

text: Adapted from the Housing First model, which was originally developed for chronically homeless, single adults struggling with mental health disorders and addictions,[13] the DVHF model includes 2 components: survivor-driven housing-inclusive advocacy and flexible funding.[11]
label: BACKGROUND

text: The former component involves advocates working proactively and creatively with survivors to help them obtain safe and stable housing, at their own pace, for as long as the survivor needs support.
label: BACKGROUND

text: Flexible funding involves assisting survivors with individual needs that are preventing them from achieving safe and stable housing.
label: BACKGROUND

text: Funding is used to help cover a myriad of expenses, including but not limited to rent, car repair, employment-related expenses, moving expenses, and safety measures.
label: BACKGROUND

text: The model was created based on evidence from 2 earlier studies: one demonstrating the effectiveness of survivor-driven advocacy on IPV survivors’ safety and mental health,[14] and one showing that flexible funding can reduce IPV survivors’ housing instability.[15]
label: BACKGROUND

text: Given that the DVHF model continues to proliferate, empirical evidence is needed to understand the extent of its effectiveness.
label: BACKGROUND

text: This study tested the hypothesis that IPV survivors who received the DVHF model would demonstrate greater improvements in housing stability, safety, and mental health compared with survivors who received services as usual (SAU) across 2 years.
label: CLAIM

text: We assessed the effects of the Toronto Site Housing First (HF) intervention on hospitalizations and emergency department (ED) visits among homeless adults with mental illness over 7 years of follow-up.
label: CLAIM

text: The Toronto Site is part of an unblinded multi-site randomized pragmatic trial of HF for homeless adults with mental illness in Canada, which followed participants up to 7 years.
label: BACKGROUND

text: Five hundred seventy-five participants were recruited and classified as having high (HN) or moderate need (MN) for mental health support services.
label: BACKGROUND

text: Each group was randomized into intervention (HF) and treatment as usual groups, and 567 (98.6%) consented to link their data to health administrative databases.
label: BACKGROUND

text: HF participants received a monthly rent supplement of $600 (Canadian) and assertive community treatment (ACT) support or intensive care management (ICM) support based on need level.
label: BACKGROUND

text: Treatment as usual (TAU) participants had access to social, housing, and health services generally available in the community.
label: BACKGROUND

text: Outcomes included all-cause and mental health-specific hospitalization, number of days in hospital, and ED visit.
label: BACKGROUND

text: We used GEE models to estimate ratio of rate ratios (RRR).
label: BACKGROUND

text: The results showed HF with ACT had no significant effect on hospitalization rates among HN participants, but reduced the number of days in hospital (RRR = 0.32, 95% CI 0.16-0.63) and number of ED visits (RRR = 0.57, 95% CI 0.34-0.95).
label: CLAIM

text: HF with ICM resulted in an increase in the number of hospitalizations (RRR = 1.69, 95% CI 1.09-2.60) and ED visit rates (RRR = 1.42, 95% CI 1.01-2.01) but had no effect in days in hospital for MN participants.
label: CLAIM

text: Addressing the health needs of this population and reducing acute care utilization remain system priorities.
label: BACKGROUND

text: People experiencing homelessness are affected by chronic and acute medical conditions [1–8], neurocognitive impairment, and substance use disorders at higher rates than the general population [1, 9–11].
label: BACKGROUND

text: The unstable living conditions associated with homelessness not only increase heath need complexity but in addition interfere with accessing primary health care and effective disease management.
label: BACKGROUND

text: It is therefore not surprising that, individuals experiencing homelessness are higher users of emergency departments (ED) [12] and are more frequently admitted to hospital compared to the general population [2, 12–14].
label: BACKGROUND

text: The provision of stable housing with supportive services has been identified as a promising intervention to decrease ED visits and hospital admissions for this population [15].
label: BACKGROUND

text: However, controlled studies of housing interventions have shown mixed effects on health care utilization [16–19].
label: BACKGROUND

text: These studies have generally used self-reported data on health care use, analyzed only a few specific health care services, or have had a relatively short period of follow-up.
label: BACKGROUND

text: These limitations have resulted in uncertainty regarding the long-term impacts of supportive housing programs on health care utilization.
label: BACKGROUND

text: The purpose of this analysis of the Toronto Site At Home/Chez-Soi randomized pragmatic study is to investigate the effects of a Housing First (HF) intervention, including immediate access to housing and mental health support services, on several acute health care utilization outcomes, including all-cause hospitalization, mental health-related hospitalizations, and ED visits, among adults experiencing homelessness and mental illness over a 7-year follow-up period.
label: CLAIM

text: This analysis leverages comprehensive provincial administrative databases and the longest HF trial to date to ascertain the health utilization outcomes of study participants over an extended follow-up period in a large urban setting with universal health insurance.
label: CLAIM

text: To determine whether a full-scale randomised control trial (RCT) assessing the efficacy and cost-effectiveness of a housing led Critical Time Intervention (CTI) is feasible and acceptable.
label: CLAIM

text: Pilot parallel two-arm individual level RCT, including process evaluation and embedded exploratory health economic evaluation.
label: BACKGROUND

text: Four prisons for men across England and Wales, UK.
label: BACKGROUND

text: Men leaving prison at risk of homelessness and intervention delivery staff.
label: BACKGROUND

text: CTI has four components: (1) pre-engagement phase: assessing the needs of the client and implementing a plan pre-discharge; (2) transition to community: forming relationships and goal setting; (3) try out: encouraging problem-solving and managing practical issues and (4) transfer of care: developing long-term goals and transferring responsibilities to community providers.
label: BACKGROUND

text: Progression criteria: recruitment, retention, acceptability of the processes (CTI and trial method) and fidelity of intervention delivery.
label: BACKGROUND

text: We also assessed the completeness of primary, secondary and exploratory outcome measures and estimated intervention costs.
label: BACKGROUND

text: The recruitment progression criterion was met, with 92% (34/37) of approached individuals consenting to participate (target: 50%).
label: CLAIM

text: However, the overall recruitment target of 80 was not achieved, and retention was low, only 18% (6/34) provided follow-up data, well below the 60% threshold.
label: CLAIM

text: Retention was hindered by systemic challenges, including changes to prison release policies and reduced probation support.
label: CLAIM

text: While the CTI model was acceptable to staff and service users, the trial design, particularly randomisation, was not.
label: CLAIM

text: Intervention fidelity met the progression criteria.
label: CLAIM

text: Baseline data collection for health economics and resource use was feasible, and intervention costs were estimated.
label: CLAIM

text: This pilot trial identified significant challenges to conducting a full-scale RCT of CTI in this context, particularly around retention, trial acceptability and systemic instability.
label: CLAIM

text: While CTI remains a promising model, a traditional RCT design may not be viable in this setting without substantial structural and ethical adaptations.
label: CLAIM

text: For people leaving prison, re-integrating into the community can be a difficult process.
label: BACKGROUND

text: The absence of suitable affordable housing and a stable support network, in the context that many may have complex needs linked to substance use and mental ill-health, makes people leaving prison more susceptible to homelessness.[1]
label: BACKGROUND

text: The absence of stable accommodation can then have further repercussions.
label: BACKGROUND

text: People experiencing homelessness are at a higher risk than the general population of infectious and non-communicable diseases, mental health problems, alcohol and substance use, have higher rates of hospital admissions and report lower levels of well-being and health-related quality of life.[1–4]
label: BACKGROUND

text: Health outcomes are substantially worse among people with a history of both imprisonment and homelessness than each in isolation.[5]
label: BACKGROUND

text: The detrimental consequences of homelessness following imprisonment can lead to a huge societal burden in terms of healthcare and societal costs.[6]
label: BACKGROUND

text: Critical Time Interventions (CTIs) are structured, time-limited case management approaches designed to support individuals during periods of transition, such as release from prison, by enhancing engagement with treatment and community services through problem-solving and continuity of care.[7]
label: BACKGROUND

text: Core components include small caseloads, active outreach, personalised case management, psychosocial skill-building and motivational support, delivered through a phased model that tapers in intensity over time.[7 8]
label: BACKGROUND

text: A multisite randomised control trial (RCT) in the UK demonstrated that CTI could be feasibly and acceptably implemented in prison settings, showing improved service engagement and providing valuable economic evaluation data.[8]
label: BACKGROUND

text: While international evidence suggests CTI may improve housing stability among people experiencing or at risk of homelessness, its impact on health outcomes and quality of life remains limited.[8–12]
label: BACKGROUND

text: Gaps remain, particularly the limited UK-based RCTs among prison-leavers facing housing instability, highlighting the need for further research in this area.
label: BACKGROUND

text: The overall aim was to conduct a pilot RCT to determine whether a future full-scale RCT assessing effectiveness and cost-effectiveness of a housing-led CTI is warranted.
label: CLAIM
